source.title: Mr. Snuffleupagus at SemEval-2025 Task 4: Unlearning Factual Knowledge from LLMs Using Adaptive RMU

record.tranche_reason: Tests adaptive RMU as an unlearning method on task-specific factual and sensitive content, using task-regurgitation and capability metrics. It does not test recovery attacks.
record.gate_note: The paper reports task-aggregate, MMLU, and MIA scores for layer combinations on OLMo-1B and method comparisons on OLMo-7B. The task aggregate combines forget- and retain-set scores, so it does not isolate targeted-knowledge accuracy or establish a near-chance value. MIA is membership-inference leakage, not recovery through the attacks in versions B–E; those results are recorded as none. No separate per-subtask forget scores are reported in the supplied text.
record.test_reason: A SemEval system paper that applies Adaptive RMU and reports only its own leaderboard metrics. These are a harmonic-mean task aggregate that mixes inverted forget scores with retain scores, an MIA score and MMLU. It reports no isolated forget-set accuracy against chance, no original-model MMLU reference, and no recovery attack (fine-tuning, ablation, quantization or prompting). Its results therefore cannot show whether targeted knowledge reaches near chance or survives attacks.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that Adaptive RMU on later (or middle-later) decoder layers is an effective way to unlearn factual and PII-type knowledge, needing little tuning, and that it ranked 4th on both leaderboards. They contrast this with original RMU's earlier layers for hazardous knowledge. The choice of layers 12-14 is driven mainly by MIA robustness, which the appendix says outweighs small losses in the aggregate and MMLU scores. The conclusion also mislabels RMU as 'Rank-One Model Update'.
record.recipe_differences: Uses Adaptive RMU, which changes the forget-loss scaling dynamically; uses the task retain set rather than an external retain dataset. Reports a sweep over three consecutive decoder layers.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported scores vary across the tested layer combinations. The authors identify layers 12,13,14 as ideal for OLMo-1B and 24,25,26 for OLMo-7B, but the supplied tables give the detailed layer sweep only for OLMo-1B.

fits_no_version.finding: MIA robustness score for Adaptive RMU varies strongly with the unlearned layer triple on OLMo-1B, from 0.062 (layers 0,1,2) to 0.835 (layers 12,13,14). The baselines also differ widely on OLMo-7B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Membership-inference leakage after RMU-style unlearning depends on which decoder layers are targeted, with later layers leaking less.

record.problems: The task aggregate does not expose forget-set scores separately, and no unlearned-model reference or chance comparison is given. The paper says experiments were conducted exclusively on the 1B model, but also provides a 7B comparison table and makes 7B claims without detailed 7B layer results. No recovery attack is evaluated.

untested.parts: Forget-set accuracy versus chance, retention relative to the original model, and resistance to any recovery attack.
No activation-direction ablation or blocking-versus-deletion analysis.
No prompting, jailbreak, language or in-context attack.
Robustness of Adaptive RMU is asserted only by citing Huu-Tien et al.; it is not evaluated here.

record.verdict_notes: Reclassified from tests/T2 to uses_without_test/T4. The paper reports only competition metrics for its own system and a few baselines, with no forget-only scores, no pre-unlearning references and no attacks. The record's 'absent'/'observed' states on the 7B MMLU rows used the task's 0.371 eligibility threshold as if it were a baseline. The 1B MMLU values are around 0.25 for every layer choice, about 4-choice chance, but without the original model's score this cannot show a capability loss. The paper says experiments ran only on the 1B model, yet it names 7B layers 24,25,26 without showing any 7B layer sweep.

versions.untested_parts: The paper evaluates task-specific regurgitation and MMLU, but does not report isolated targeted-knowledge accuracy against chance, an unlearned-model baseline for these scores, or whether recovery attacks succeed.
No activation-direction ablation or analysis establishing blocking rather than deletion.
No prompt rephrasing, jailbreak, language, or in-context recovery attack.
Adaptive RMU is discussed as robust to adversarial attacks, but the paper reports no own attack-resistance evaluation.
